title: Instruct the ignorant
tomorrow: how do you tell a king he's wrong and keep your head?

lines: GRAB THE MOUSE, OR PULL UP A CHAIR?
HOW CAN I, UNLESS SOME MAN SHEW ME?
cards: Two kinds of help. One coworker grabs your mouse, clicks four times, says see? and leaves you knowing nothing. Another pulls up a chair and asks where you got stuck.

In the book of Acts, an official of the queen of Ethiopia sits in his chariot on a desert road, reading the prophet Isaiah, and he's stuck. A man named Philip runs up alongside and asks if he understands what he reads.
The answer, in the Douay-Rheims: "And how can I, unless some man shew me?"

teach.b: What he needed most wasn't a smarter book. It was someone beside him. And notice the old word in this work of mercy.
Ignorant here doesn't mean foolish. It means not knowing. This man is no fool; Acts says he had charge of all the queen's treasure, and he's reading Isaiah on the road home.
He runs to catch up; the learner doesn't have to come to him. He asks a question before he explains anything. He climbs up only when he's invited.
And Acts says that, beginning at that very scripture, Philip told him about Jesus.

teach.h: HE STARTS ON THE MAN'S OWN PAGE.
teach.b: He started on the page the man was already on. Soon the man sees water by the road and asks to be baptized. Then Philip is gone, and the man goes on his way rejoicing.
The teacher doesn't stay at the center.
Peter's first letter adds the tone: be ready to give a reason for your hope, "But with modesty and fear." Humbly, in other words.
The Church lists instructing the ignorant among the spiritual works of mercy. In a parish, that's catechists teaching children, and adults who want to join the Church.
But it's wider than a classroom: showing a new teammate the drill, teaching a kid a family recipe, explaining a prayer to a curious friend. Catch up, ask first, start on their page, then step back.

how: Catholic parishes rely on volunteer catechists to teach children and to prepare adults who want to join the Church, and Catholics also take on this work informally at home and at work.

o: correct people who think they're smart
run a Catholic school for children
teach someone who doesn't know yet

games.q: the chariot on the desert road — tap the pairs.
p: ran the queen's treasury, stuck on Isaiah
ran to catch up and asked first

s: in this work of mercy, ignorant means foolish
it means not knowing. the man in the chariot ran the queen's treasury.
Philip stayed on as the official's teacher
after the baptism Philip was gone, and the man went on his way rejoicing.
Philip climbed into the chariot only after he was invited
he asked a question first and waited to be asked up.

games.q: a new kid on your team keeps running the wrong side of a drill, and the coach is busy. what would Philip do?
o: jog alongside, ask what she thinks the drill is for, start there.
shout the right spot across the field so she learns it fast.
leave it; she'll pick it up from watching the others in time.
games.why: Philip ran to catch up, asked a question first, and began from the scripture the man was already reading.

practice: Pick one thing you know how to do: a recipe, a move, a prayer, a shortcut. Out loud, explain its first step as if to someone beside you who has never seen it, slowly and in plain words.
Then sit quietly with the person you'd most like to teach it to, and if you pray, you can pray for them.

wordCard.voice: Instruct the ignorant. Teach someone who doesn't know yet, starting where they are, and humbly.

orig.note: Greek: will guide. the official's word in Acts 8:31, unless someone guides me.

carryVoice: Your line: share what you know. Philip ran to catch up, then let the learner lead. Until tomorrow.
